newsitem.title: INDIA: Non-aligned nations meet in India to discuss UN.
newsitem.headline: Non-aligned nations meet in India to discuss UN.

text.p: The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), plagued by doubts about its relevance in the post-Cold War world, will issue a demand for greater clout in the United Nations at a two-day conference in the Indian capital this week.

Permanent representation for one or more of its member states on the powerful U.N. Security Council would go a long way towards dispelling the lingering view that NAM is long on membership but short on usefulness, delegates said.
"There is a refrain in some quarters that NAM has outlived its role or has no cohesion," the 113-nation NAM said in a background paper for the meeting of foreign ministers which starts on Monday.
"Such views are either motivated or based on a misperception."
NAM was launched in Belgrade in 1961, a product of a bipolar world pitting the Soviet Union and its Warsaw Pact allies against United States and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
With the disintegration of the Soviet Union and the cooling of East-West tensions, NAM lost a motivating force.
"Armchair analysts seem to believe NAM no longer has a raison d'etre," Colombian ambassador to the U.N. Julio Londono Paredes told senior NAM officials last week.
"It's a wonder it hasn't died," said one Western diplomat.
But NAM officials said membership had grown from 25 in 1961 to 113 today, reflecting continued concern at unequal distribution of the world's economic and political power.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan was asked on Saturday to comment on critics who say NAM has lost its relevance. "I disagree with them, and they will find out in the course of the week," he told Reuters in the Indian capital.
Annan, along with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, was to address NAM foreign ministers on Monday.
More than 70 foreign ministers were expected in the capital of India, one of the movement's founding members. Other countries were sending senior officials.

NAM currently has 113 members, ranging from Afghanistan to Zimbabwe, but Yugoslavia's membership is in suspension. Russia and eight NATO members are guests of NAM, currently chaired by Colombia. South Africa was expected to take over the chairmanship from Colombia before the next NAM summit.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan was to attend and hold bilateral talks with his Indian counterpart, Inder Kumar Gujral, on Wednesday morning after the NAM meeting ends.
One of the main themes to be discussed this week is an expansion of the U.N. Security Council, officials said.
The draft final document to be taken up on Monday says "the under-representation of Non-Aligned and developing countries in the Council should be corrected by its enlargement".
The five current permanent members -- Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States -- are also the world's five declared nuclear powers.
The draft NAM document also calls for the curtailing of the right of permanent members to veto council decisions.

The theme fits in nicely with India's campaign to clinch a permanent seat on the council. But NAM member states were divided over the degree to which the Security Council veto should be curbed and criteria for selecting permanent members.
Other key issues to be debated are nuclear disarmament, the environment and economic development, delegates said.
